items.summary: Processing language and truly understanding it are two different things. Here is the line between them, and the bigger ambition sitting behind both. Terms covered: - NLP (Natural Language Processing): translating, classifying, extracting and detecting sentiment. Taking raw text and doing something meaningful with it. - NLU (Natural Language Understanding): a subset of NLP focused on intent, meaning and context. Recognizing that "I want to cancel" signals a customer about to churn, not just four words typed. - AGI (Artificial General Intelligence): a hypothetical AI that reasons and performs across any domain the way a human can From processing, to understanding, to reasoning. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #NLP #NLU #AGI #AIGlossary #H2Oai

items.title: 100x More Reliable Voice Agents
items.summary: Luke and Nico work at SLNG.ai. Today they launch Unmute, an open declarative standard for voice agents, under an MIT license. The problem they are attacking: every voice agent platform has its own definition of what an agent is. Build on ElevenLabs, VAPI, Retell or Bolna and your agent stays there. Even across the open frameworks, a Pipecat agent does not port cleanly to LiveKit. You pick a stack, you build inside it, and your voice IP ends up owned by whichever one you started with. - Three assumptions Unmute argues are wrong: that voice agents are a sequential turn-taking pipeline, that the LLM should be the decision-making spine of the call, and that you must choose between rigid IVR and a long prompt followed by hope - Declared execution: tool calls, data flows, step transitions and failure handling are declared and enforced by the compiled package, and the LLM becomes an optional resource that has to earn its place - Determinism as a dial, set turn by turn. Lock a regulatory disclosure, leave an open-ended objection generative, in the same call - Why single-prompt agents break: the model reads every rule at every turn, goes off topic, picks some rules and ignores others, and nobody can tell which part caused the failure - The salon example, built twice. On the left, one agent, one prompt, ten tool descriptions read on every turn, and a section whose only job is telling the model which of four steps it is on. On the right, a concierge with one tool and a separate complaint specialist - The measured result in Langfuse: same conversation, same step count, but more than double the token usage on the single-prompt version, plus fewer turns and lower latency on the split one - The counterintuitive part: the four split prompts contain nearly double the total text, but you only pay for what sits in front of the model right now. Someone asking what time you open should not pay for the refund policy - Structural guarantees over instructions: the booking step is not handed to the model until a confirmed number exists, so a booking without confirmation is impossible rather than merely unlikely - Prefetch before the greeting. Luke and Nico work at SLNG.ai. Today they launch Unmute, an open declarative standard for voice agents, under an MIT license.

The problem they are attacking: every voice agent platform has its own definition of what an agent is. Build on ElevenLabs, VAPI, Retell or Bolna and your agent stays there. Even across the open frameworks, a Pipecat agent does not port cleanly to LiveKit. You pick a stack, you build inside it, and your voice IP ends up owned by whichever one you started with.

- Three assumptions Unmute argues are wrong: that voice agents are a sequential turn-taking pipeline, that the LLM should be the decision-making spine of the call, and that you must choose between rigid IVR and a long prompt followed by hope
- Declared execution: tool calls, data flows, step transitions and failure handling are declared and enforced by the compiled package, and the LLM becomes an optional resource that has to earn its place
- Determinism as a dial, set turn by turn. Lock a regulatory disclosure, leave an open-ended objection generative, in the same call
- Why single-prompt agents break: the model reads every rule at every turn, goes off topic, picks some rules and ignores others, and nobody can tell which part caused the failure
- The salon example, built twice. On the left, one agent, one prompt, ten tool descriptions read on every turn, and a section whose only job is telling the model which of four steps it is on. On the right, a concierge with one tool and a separate complaint specialist
